rules.statement: When a change removes the behavior a variable, function or block was named for, rename it, and its loop variables, after what it does now.
rules.why: A name kept from removed behavior makes readers think the code still does the old job.
rules.check: Look in the diff for identifiers that still name a feature, rule or check the diff removes but that now serve a different purpose.

rules.statement: Before reporting that a coupling or detection heuristic would break silently with no test catching it, check whether existing tests already assert the observable outcome, and don't report it when they do.
rules.why: The maintainer declined such a finding because tests already asserted the output each branch produces, so renaming or moving the matched element would already fail the suite.
rules.check: Search the test suite for assertions on the output or behavior that depends on the match, covering both the positive and the fallback case, before raising the finding.

rules.statement: Don't ask for tests that assert the absence of hypothetical future additions, such as a key or condition the code doesn't have today, when the existing tests already pin what the change is about.
rules.why: The maintainer declined this because such assertions pin the code's shape further than the change needs.
rules.check: When proposing an extra assertion, confirm that it guards behavior the diff introduces or changes, not a speculative future edit.

rules.statement: When a change alters behavior that downstream users will notice, such as when CI triggers run, say so in the pull request description, not only in the CHANGELOG.
rules.why: Reviewers who read only the description would miss a behavior change that downstream projects will see.
rules.check: Compare the user-visible behavior changes in the diff, such as removed triggers, changed defaults or dropped checks, with the PR description, and flag any that it leaves out.
